519.title: Looking back: no excuse
519.hook: a discourse we passed: Sariputta tells a brahmin that duty to family does not excuse harming others
519.howItsDone: Buddhist ethics across schools honors support for parents and family as a duty while holding that right livelihood, earning without harming others, is part of the eightfold path; teachers often cite MN 97 on this point.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ghatikara and his blind parents, and your line, the good potter. Did you do one task with honest hands? Today, another discourse we walked past, and a man who wasn't so honest. Day five hundred nineteen.

I'm doing it for my family. It's one of the oldest sentences there is, and it's said about the best things people do, and sometimes about the worst. In the ninety-seventh discourse, Sariputta hears news about an old acquaintance, a brahmin named Dhananjani who works for the king. He's gotten careless, people say. He uses the king's authority to squeeze the brahmin householders, and uses the householders as cover to cheat the king. Sariputta goes to find him. Today, looking back: no excuse.
screen: `I'M DOING IT FOR MY FAMILY.` → `DHANANJANI, THE KING'S MAN.` → `SARIPUTTA GOES TO FIND HIM.`

segments.voice: Sariputta finds him at a cowshed while the cows are being milked. Dhananjani offers him fresh milk. Sariputta says he's already eaten for the day, and asks: Dhananjani, are you diligent? How can I be? the brahmin answers. I have my parents to support. A wife and children. Workers. Duties to friends, to ancestors, to the gods, to the king. And this body has to be fed too. It's an honest list, and a heavy one. Sariputta doesn't dismiss it. He asks a question instead. Suppose a man did harm, broke the moral law, for his parents' sake. And suppose that when he died, the wardens of the hell realms dragged him off. Could he say: I did it for my parents, let me go? Could his parents say: he did it for us, let him go? No, says Dhananjani. Then the same question, one by one. For wife and children? For workers? Friends? Ancestors? The gods? The king? For this body? No, every time. Sariputta asks one more. Who's better: the one who does wrong for his parents, or the one who does right for them? The one who does right. Then there are other ways, Sariputta says, ways in line with the dhamma, to earn a living, support your parents, and not do harm. The Pali word is dhammika: righteous, in keeping with the dhamma. The point isn't that family duty is bad. In the discourses it's honored again and again. The point is that love for your own doesn't turn harm to others into something else. The duty stays. The excuse goes.
screen: `AT THE COWSHED, MILK OFFERED` · `I HAVE SO MANY TO SUPPORT` · `COULD HE SAY: I DID IT FOR THEM?` · `THERE ARE RIGHTEOUS WAYS` · then, large: `NO EXCUSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check one excuse you use. Sit quietly and let one come up. Maybe it's I'm too busy, or everyone does it, or it's for the kids. Hold it gently, the way Sariputta held Dhananjani's list. Is the duty real? Probably yes. Now ask: is there a way to meet it without the harm? Don't solve it all. Just see one other way. The bell holds the time.
Looking back. A second discourse we passed: duty to family is real, but it never makes harming others right. Today's word.
Your line: no excuse. Today, when you hear yourself say I had to, ask once whether there was a kinder way to do the same duty. Day five hundred nineteen.

520.title: Your favorite discourse
520.hook: of the Majjhima read so far, which one stays
520.howItsDone: Many Buddhists return to a few discourses again and again; in Theravada communities some are chanted as paritta for protection and blessing, and teachers often assign students one discourse to study closely for a long time.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dhananjani at the cowshed, and your line, no excuse. Did you find a kinder way to meet one duty? Today, no new discourse. Just a question for you. Day five hundred twenty.

About four months ago we opened the Middle-Length Sayings. Since then: a raft, a saw, a snake grabbed by the tail. A hen sitting on her eggs. A murderer turned monk. A fire that goes out and goes nowhere. Seven chariots in relay. A potter's roof. Most of it has blurred, the way books do. But something probably stuck. One picture you've thought about in the shower, or told a friend. Today: your favorite discourse.
screen: `A RAFT, A SAW, A SNAKE.` → `A HEN, A FIRE, SEVEN CHARIOTS.` → `WHICH ONE STAYED?`

segments.voice: Having a favorite isn't a modern habit. The word for a discourse is sutta, which many explain as a thread, the Pali form of the Sanskrit sutra. A thread is something you can pick up again. And Buddhist communities have always picked up some threads more than others. In Theravada countries, certain discourses are chanted for protection and blessing. Teachers return again and again to a handful, like the one on mindfulness of breathing, or the verse about one fine night: don't chase the past, don't pin hopes on the future. The discourses themselves suggest why. Remember the day we counted feelings: two, three, five, six, eighteen, a hundred and eight. The Buddha said each count was a way of teaching, fitted to the listener. Different people needed different doors. So a favorite isn't a ranking of the teaching. It's a clue about where you are. If the saw stayed with you, maybe you're working with anger. If it was the raft, maybe with holding on too tight to ideas. If it was the hen on her eggs, maybe with patience. There's a caution too, and it comes from the water snake discourse. Grab a teaching by the wrong end and it bites. So the question isn't only which line do I like, but how am I holding it. The best test of a favorite is the one the old monks used: go back and read it whole. Not the quote you remember, the full discourse, with its setting and its questions. Often it says more, or something slightly different, than the version you've been carrying.
screen: `SUTTA: A THREAD TO PICK UP` · `COMMUNITIES HAVE FAVORITES TOO` · `A FAVORITE SHOWS WHERE YOU ARE` · `READ IT WHOLE AGAIN` · then, large: `YOURS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: reread one discourse, starting now, in your mind. Close your eyes and let one picture from these months rise. Don't choose the impressive one. Choose the one that comes. Where was it set? Who asked the question? What was the image? Sit with it, and notice what it says to you today. Later, if you can, find the full text and read it through. The bell holds the time.
Your favorite discourse. The thread that stayed with you, a clue to where you are, best tested by reading it whole again. Today's word.
Your line: yours. Today, tell one person about the image that stayed with you, and notice what you say about it. Day five hundred twenty.

521.title: The Middle-Length, closed
521.hook: from the root of all things to the training of the senses
521.howItsDone: The Majjhima Nikaya is one of the five collections of the Sutta Pitaka in the Pali Canon, studied and recited in Theravada monasteries; many of its discourses have parallels in the Chinese Madhyama Agama preserved by other early schools.

segments.voice: Yesterday: your favorite discourse, and your line, yours. Which image did you tell someone about? Today we close the whole Middle-Length collection. Day five hundred twenty-one.

The first discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings ends with something you almost never read in these texts: the monks were not pleased. The teaching on the root of all things was too hard, or too sharp. The last discourse ends with a young brahmin sitting silent and a quiet teaching about eyes that stay open. In between, a hundred and fifty more. Today, the whole shelf, from the first to the last. Today: the Middle-Length, closed.
screen: `THE FIRST: THE MONKS WERE NOT PLEASED.` → `THE LAST: EYES THAT STAY OPEN.` → `A HUNDRED AND FIFTY IN BETWEEN.`

segments.voice: The Pali name is Majjhima Nikaya: the middle collection. Middle here means middle-length. Not as long as the long discourses, not as short as the connected ones. It's arranged in three groups of fifty, the root fifty, the middle fifty and the last fifty, and the last group has two extra, which is how you get a hundred and fifty-two. Here's the road we walked. The root of all things, and all the taints. Heirs in dhamma, not in things. Fear met in the forest at night. The stained cloth that won't take the dye. The saw, and goodwill even under it. The water snake and the raft. Relay chariots. The noble search. Milk and water. Saccaka sweating. Examine even the teacher. Rahula and the mirror, then the earth. Angulimala, read whole. Any wood makes fire. Breathing in sixteen steps. A hall empty of elephants. One fine night. Punna going west. Rahula freed under a tree, six sets of six, and finally, seeing without being swept. Now here's the small surprise in the name. Majjhima is the same word as the middle in the middle way, majjhima patipada, the path between indulgence and self-torment that the Buddha named in his first teaching. The title is about length, not doctrine. But the collection keeps showing that path anyway: not grabbing, not pushing away, not shutting the eyes, not drowning in what they see. A hundred and fifty-two ways of walking down the middle, in words.
screen: `MAJJHIMA: THE MIDDLE COLLECTION` · `THREE FIFTIES, PLUS TWO` · `FROM THE ROOT TO THE SENSES` · `THE SAME WORD AS THE MIDDLE WAY` · then, large: `THE MIDDLE WAY, IN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with one line. Choose one from the whole collection, whichever comes: the raft is for crossing. All of it changing. Empty of this. See and stay. Say it once, quietly, and then let it go silent. When the mind wanders, bring back just the line, and then the quiet again. Not grabbing it, not pushing it away. The bell holds the time.
The Middle-Length. The Majjhima Nikaya, a hundred and fifty-two discourses, from the root of all things to the training of the senses. Today's word.

Your line: the middle way, in words. Today, when you're pulled toward too much or too little, look for the middle, and remember a hundred and fifty-two discourses looking for it too. Day five hundred twenty-one.

522.title: The Long Discourses
522.hook: thirty-four long discourses, many set as stories and conversations
522.howItsDone: The Digha Nikaya is the first of the five collections of discourses in the Pali Canon; Theravada monastics study it, and some of its discourses, like the one on the foundations of mindfulness, are recited and taught widely across Buddhist schools.

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed the Middle-Length Sayings, with your line, the middle way, in words. Where did you find a middle? Today a new shelf, with fewer books and longer ones. Day five hundred twenty-two.

A king on his palace roof on a full-moon night, asking his ministers which teacher to visit. A brahmin with hundreds of animals tied up for a sacrifice. A monk climbing through heaven after heaven with a question no god can answer. The Buddha's last journey, step by step, to the grove where he lay down for the last time. These are all in one collection, and it's only thirty-four discourses long. Today: the Long Discourses.
screen: `A KING ON A MOONLIT ROOF.` → `A MONK CLIMBING THROUGH HEAVENS.` → `THE LAST JOURNEY.`

segments.voice: The Pali name is Digha Nikaya, the long collection. Digha just means long. Thirty-four discourses, some of them as long as a short book. It comes in three parts. The first, thirteen discourses, is named for morality, because each one contains the same long passage on a monk's conduct. The second, the great division, holds the big set pieces: the Buddha's final days, the great discourse on the foundations of mindfulness. The third gathers the rest, including the advice to a young householder named Sigala on how to treat parents, teachers, spouse, friends and workers. Where the Middle-Length Sayings often talk to monks, the long ones often talk to outsiders. Kings, wealthy brahmins, wandering philosophers, a curious householder. Many are stories with a setting and a plot: someone arrives with a question, a challenge, sometimes a grudge, and leaves changed, or not. Some scholars suggest this collection was especially suited to presenting the teaching to people who weren't yet followers. That's a theory, and others weigh it differently. In English, an early translation of these discourses came from Thomas Rhys Davids, later joined by Caroline Rhys Davids, under the title Dialogues of the Buddha, starting in 1899. That name fits. Over the next weeks we'll read the first thirteen in order: praise and blame, the net of views, a king's moonlit ride, a proud young brahmin, a sacrifice with no blood, the line of the blind. Long discourses, taken a piece at a time.
screen: `DIGHA: LONG, THIRTY-FOUR OF THEM` · `THREE PARTS: MORALITY, GREAT, THE REST` · `OFTEN SPEAKING TO OUTSIDERS` · `DIALOGUES, TAKEN A PIECE AT A TIME` · then, large: `THE LONG ONES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read the list of titles, the way you'd read a menu. Here are a few. The supreme net. The fruits of the contemplative life. The great discourse on the final passing. The great discourse on the foundations of mindfulness. The advice to Sigala. Close your eyes. Which one pulled at you, even a little? Don't decide why. Just notice the pull, and rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Digha Nikaya. The long collection: thirty-four discourses, many told as stories and conversations with kings, brahmins and wanderers. Today's word.
Your line: the long ones. Today, give one conversation more time than usual, and let it run long. Day five hundred twenty-two.

523.title: Praise and blame
523.hook: if others praise or blame the Buddha, the monks should be neither elated nor angry
523.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers across schools speak of the eight worldly winds (gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, pleasure and pain), and practitioners train to meet them with equanimity, as the opening of DN 1 describes.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Digha Nikaya, and your line, the long ones. Did one conversation run longer than usual? Today the long collection begins, on a dusty road. Day five hundred twenty-three.

The first long discourse starts on the road between Rajagaha and Nalanda. The Buddha is walking with a large group of monks. Behind them, on the same road, come two more travelers: a wandering teacher named Suppiya and his young student Brahmadatta. And all the way, they're arguing. Suppiya is running down the Buddha, his teaching and his monks. His own student is praising all three. Teacher and pupil, walking right behind, saying opposite things. That night everyone stops at the same rest house. Today: praise and blame.
screen: `THE ROAD TO NALANDA.` → `ONE BLAMES, ONE PRAISES.` → `THE SAME REST HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Next morning, the monks are talking it over. Amazing, isn't it, the two of them, one praising and one blaming, all the way down the road. The Buddha walks in and asks what they're discussing. Then he gives the instruction that opens the whole long collection. If others speak against me, he says, or against the teaching, or against the community, don't be angry or resentful or upset. Why not? First, because it would be an obstacle for you. And second, because if you were angry, could you even tell whether what they said was true or false? The monks admit they couldn't. So instead, he says, if something said is false, calmly explain that it's false: that isn't so, that isn't found among us. And then the other half, which is easier to miss. If others speak in praise of me, or the teaching, or the community, don't be elated or delighted or puffed up. That too would be an obstacle. If what they say is true, simply acknowledge it: yes, that's so, that's found among us. The Pali words are vanna and avanna: praise and dispraise. Notice the symmetry. Praise is treated as just as risky as blame. Both cloud the mind, and a clouded mind can't check facts. The instruction isn't to stop caring what's true. It's the opposite. Stay level, so you can see what's true. And the monks are told to do it for their own teacher, not just for themselves. Even loyalty is supposed to stay calm.
screen: `THE MONKS TALK IT OVER` · `BLAME: DON'T BE ANGRY` · `PRAISE: DON'T BE ELATED` · `STAY LEVEL TO SEE WHAT'S TRUE` · then, large: `NOT ELATED, NOT ANGRY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay level at praise. Remember a compliment you got recently. Let it play back. Notice the lift in the chest, the warm glow. Don't push it away. Just ask: is it true? Part of it? All of it? Now remember a criticism, a small one. Notice the drop, the heat. Ask the same question: is it true? Part? Let both sit side by side, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Praise and blame. Vanna and avanna. Neither to be angry at nor elated by, so the mind stays clear enough to tell what's true. Today's word.
Your line: not elated, not angry. Today, when praise or blame comes your way, pause and ask only: what here is true? Day five hundred twenty-three.

524.title: The small things
524.hook: the Buddha refrains from even small unkindness, like idle talk and shows
524.howItsDone: Lay Buddhists in many traditions keep five precepts, and on observance days some take eight, which add refraining from entertainments, adornment and luxurious beds: a lay echo of the conduct listed in DN 1.

segments.voice: Yesterday: praise and blame on the road, and your line, not elated, not angry. What was true in the praise or blame you met? Today, what people actually praise the Buddha for. Day five hundred twenty-four.

Board games on eight-row and ten-row boards. Games played on imaginary boards in the air. Dice. Toy plows and toy windmills. Guessing what a friend is thinking. Elephant fights, ballad singers, acrobats. This is a real list, from the first long discourse, and it's a snapshot of what people did for fun two and a half thousand years ago. It's there because the Buddha is describing what he doesn't do. And, he says, these little things are what most people praise him for. Today: the small things.
screen: `DICE, BOARD GAMES, ELEPHANT FIGHTS.` → `A SNAPSHOT OF ANCIENT FUN.` → `WHAT PEOPLE PRAISE HIM FOR.`

segments.voice: After yesterday's teaching on praise and blame, the Buddha says something surprising. When an ordinary person praises me, he tells the monks, it's for small matters, mere moral conduct. Then he lists them. He's put down the stick and the sword. He's gentle and kind, trembling for the welfare of all living beings. He takes only what's given. He speaks the truth, he's reliable. He doesn't carry tales from one group to another to split them apart. He brings together those who are divided, and he enjoys harmony. His speech isn't harsh. It's pleasant to the ear, it goes to the heart. He doesn't waste words. He speaks at the right time, about what's true and useful. Then the finer points. He doesn't damage seeds or plants. He doesn't go to shows: dancing, singing, music, those elephant fights. He doesn't play the games. He doesn't trade in false weights and measures. He doesn't pass the day in what the text calls low talk: talk of kings and robbers, food and clothes, gossip at the well. The Pali word for all this is sila: moral conduct, virtue. And here's the twist. The Buddha calls it small. The real teaching, he says, is deeper, and the rest of the discourse goes there. But notice that he practices every one of the small things anyway. The small things aren't the summit. They're the ground the summit stands on. Kind speech, no gossip, careful hands. The list is long, and almost every item is small enough to do today.
screen: `WHAT ORDINARY PEOPLE PRAISE` · `NO STICK, NO SWORD, NO TALE-BEARING` · `NO SHOWS, NO GAMES, NO LOW TALK` · `SMALL, BUT THE GROUND OF IT ALL` · then, large: `THE SMALL THINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: refine one small habit. Go through the list slowly in your mind. Gentle speech. No carrying tales. Speaking at the right time. Not wasting words. Taking only what's given. Let one of them light up, the one closest to your actual life. Picture the moment today when it will come up. See yourself doing the small thing a little better. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The small things. Sila, moral conduct, in its smallest forms: kind speech, no gossip, careful hands. Small, and still practiced. Today's word.
Your line: the small things. Today, when a bit of gossip starts, don't carry it on to the next person. Day five hundred twenty-four.

525.title: The net of views
525.hook: sixty-two views caught like fish in a fine net
525.howItsDone: The Brahmajala Sutta is studied in Theravada monasteries as a survey of speculative views; across Buddhist schools, teachers use it to show practitioners how views arise from feeling and craving rather than to promote a rival theory.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dice and elephant fights, and your line, the small things. Did you let one piece of gossip stop with you? Today ends a week, and the first long discourse throws its net. Day five hundred twenty-five.

Is the world eternal? Did it begin by chance? Is the self the same after death? Will it be destroyed? Questions like these filled the air in the Buddha's India. Wandering philosophers built whole careers on them. And some of those questions are still argued over kitchen tables and on podcasts. The first long discourse, after the small things, turns to the deep things: every theory about self and world the Buddha could name. He counts them. Sixty-two. Today: the net of views.
screen: `IS THE WORLD ETERNAL?` → `WANDERERS ARGUING EVERYWHERE.` → `SIXTY-TWO VIEWS.`

segments.voice: The views fall into two groups. Eighteen are about the past: theories that self and world are eternal, or partly eternal, or finite, or infinite, or that they arose by chance. There are even the eel-wrigglers, who slip out of every question without committing to anything. Forty-four are about the future: theories that the self survives death with perception, or without it, or is destroyed, or that the highest bliss is found right here in pleasure or in meditation. The Buddha describes each one with care, and how people arrive at it. Some through deep meditation that shows them a slice of the past and then generalize from it. Some through reasoning alone. Then comes the turn. Every one of these views, he says, depends on contact: the senses meeting the world. From contact, feeling. From feeling, craving. And from craving, clinging to a view. The Pali word is ditthi: view, opinion, literally something seen. And here's the image. Picture a skilled fisherman casting a fine-meshed net over a small pond. He knows that whatever fish of any size are in that pond, they're all inside the net. When they rise, they rise inside it. So with these sixty-two views: whoever theorizes about the past or the future is caught inside this net, however they thrash. And the one who sees how views arise, the discourse says, isn't caught. Not because he holds a sixty-third view, but because he understands the net. Look back at the week: no excuse, yours, the middle way, the long ones, not elated, not angry, the small things. And now the net that holds every theory.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: catch one of your views in the net. Pick an opinion you hold strongly. About politics, about people, about how the world works. Don't argue for or against it. Just watch it. Where does it seem to live in the body? What feeling sits under it, pleasant or tense? Is there wanting there? See the view as something that arose. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The net of views. Sixty-two theories of self and world, all arising from contact, feeling and craving, all held in one fine net. Today's word.
Your line: all views, in the net. Today, when you catch yourself defending an opinion hard, notice the feeling under it before you say the next word. Day five hundred twenty-five.

original.note: Pali ditthi (Sanskrit drishti): view, opinion, literally 'something seen'.

trapdoor: what you thought: the net of views is a list of wrong opinions.
what it means: it's a map of how theories about self and world arise, and how not to be caught by them.
what a scholar hears: the title, Brahmajala, means 'supreme net' or 'Brahma's net'; Ananda is told it may also be called the net of meaning, the net of dhamma, or the supreme victory in battle.
